title: Jeremiah 41:1–10
context: Jeremiah 41:1–10 is told by the narrator and reports Ishmael’s violence at Mizpah, which these notes describe soberly. In the seventh month Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, “of the royal offspring and one of the chief officers of the king”, comes to Mizpah with ten men, eats with Gedaliah, and then kills him, together with the Jews and Chaldean soldiers there (41:1–3; compare 2 Kings 25:25, which names the month and the royal descent). The year is not stated, and readers differ on whether these events followed the fall of Jerusalem closely or some time later. Zechariah 8:19 mentions a fast of the seventh month, which later Jewish tradition associated with Gedaliah’s death, though Zechariah does not say so. Two days later, eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria come in mourning with offerings for the LORD’s house (41:4–5); their shaved beards, torn clothes, and cuttings are signs of grief, and readers commonly take them to be bringing offerings to the site of the ruined temple. Ishmael meets them weeping, draws them into the city, and kills them, sparing ten who promise him hidden stores of food (41:6–8). He fills with the dead the pit, commonly taken to be a cistern, that King Asa had made “for fear of Baasha king of Israel” (41:9; compare 1 Kings 15:22, where Asa builds Mizpah). He then carries away the remaining people, including the king’s daughters, toward the Ammonites (41:10). The text links Ishmael with the royal line and with Baalis king of the Ammonites (40:14) but does not fully state his motives; resentment at a governor appointed by Babylon is often suggested, and these notes hold it as a suggestion. Both traditions read the passage as a grievous account of treachery against a fragile remnant.

verses.text: Now in the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the royal offspring and one of the chief officers of the king, and ten men with him, came to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam to Mizpah; and there they ate bread together in Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes: In the seventh month Ishmael, of the royal offspring and one of the king’s chief officers, came with ten men to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and they ate bread together. Arminian readers note the betrayal of hospitality, and they compare 2 Kings 25:25, named without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the shared meal makes the coming treachery especially grievous. They observe that the year is not stated and that Ishmael’s royal descent may bear on his motives, though the text does not say so directly, and they hold such suggestions loosely.

verses.text: Then Ishmael the son of Nethaniah arose, and the ten men who were with him, and struck Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmael and his ten men struck Gedaliah with the sword and killed him, the governor whom the king of Babylon had appointed. Arminian readers note the sober report of the killing and see in it the collapse of the fragile order that had given the remnant hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator records the murder plainly, without elaboration. They read it as a grievous act of treachery against a man who had refused to believe ill of his killer, and they see the remnant’s hope of stability destroyed by human violence.

verses.text: Ishmael also killed all the Jews who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean men of war who were found there.
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmael also killed all the Jews with Gedaliah at Mizpah and the Chaldean men of war found there. Arminian readers note the widening circle of violence, and they read the verse soberly, observing that the killing of the Chaldean soldiers would bring fear of reprisal on the whole remnant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 25:25 reports the same killings briefly, named without harmonizing. They observe that all the Jews may refer to those in Gedaliah’s immediate company, since others remain alive in 41:10, and they do not press the phrase further than the text allows.

verses.text: The second day after he had killed Gedaliah, and no man knew it,
verses.arminianNotes: On the second day after Gedaliah’s death, no one yet knew of it. Arminian readers note that the narrator emphasizes secrecy, setting the scene for further treachery, and they see how hidden violence can multiply when no one is aware of what has been done.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the brief verse heightens the suspense of the account. They read it as preparing for the arrival of the pilgrims, who come without knowing what has happened, and they observe that the narrator tells the story with restraint.

verses.text: men came from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, even eighty men, having their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and having cut themselves, with meal offerings and frankincense in their hand, to bring them to the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Eighty men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, with shaved beards, torn clothes, and cuttings, bringing offerings and frankincense to the LORD’s house. Arminian readers note that these signs of mourning show grief, and that they are commonly taken to be bringing offerings to the site of the ruined temple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reading and observe that the pilgrims come from the north, the old territory of Israel. They hold open the details of their purpose and route, and they read their devotion as all the more poignant in light of what is about to happen to them.

verses.text: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping all along as he went, and as he met them, he said to them, “Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmael went out weeping to meet them and said, “Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.” Arminian readers note the deceit of feigned grief, and they see in Ishmael a man who uses the appearance of mourning to lure the unsuspecting pilgrims into danger.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ishmael’s weeping may be pretended, though the text simply reports it. They read the invitation as a cruel use of Gedaliah’s name, and they observe that the narrator presents the deception soberly without dwelling on it.

verses.text: It was so, when they came into the middle of the city, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah killed them, and cast them into the middle of the pit, he, and the men who were with him.
verses.arminianNotes: When they came into the middle of the city, Ishmael and his men killed them and cast them into the pit. Arminian readers read this soberly as a terrible act against pilgrims who came to worship, and they see in it how far violence can go once restraint and fear of God have been abandoned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the massacre soberly and without detail beyond what the text gives. They observe that the narrator does not explain why Ishmael killed the pilgrims, and they hold any suggestions about his reasons loosely, as the text leaves them unstated.

verses.text: But ten men were found among those who said to Ishmael, “Don’t kill us; for we have stores hidden in the field, of wheat, and of barley, and of oil, and of honey.” So he stopped, and didn’t kill them among their brothers.
verses.arminianNotes: Ten men said to Ishmael, “Don’t kill us; for we have stores hidden in the field”, and he spared them. Arminian readers note that the men’s lives were spared for the sake of food, and they see a grim picture of how greed could interrupt even a killer’s purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same detail and read it as showing the scarcity of food after the siege, which made hidden stores valuable. They observe that the verse adds realism to the account without explaining Ishmael’s wider motives, which the text does not fully state.

verses.text: Now the pit in which Ishmael cast all the dead bodies of the men whom he had killed, by the side of Gedaliah (this was that which Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel), Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with those who were killed.
verses.arminianNotes: The pit into which Ishmael cast the dead was the one King Asa had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel. Arminian readers note the link with 1 Kings 15:22, where Asa built Mizpah, named without harmonizing, and they see history’s layers in a single place of tragedy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link and observe that the pit, once part of Asa’s defensive works, becomes a place of death. They read the verse soberly, noting that 1 Kings 15:22 does not itself mention this pit, so the connection rests on this verse’s own report.

verses.text: Then Ishmael carried away captive all of the people who were left in Mizpah, even the king’s daughters, and all the people who remained in Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah carried them away captive, and departed to go over to the children of Ammon.
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmael carried away captive all the people left in Mizpah, including the king’s daughters, and set out for the Ammonites. Arminian readers note that the captives included those Nebuzaradan had entrusted to Gedaliah, and they see the remnant’s fragile life overturned once again by violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the destination, the Ammonites, links Ishmael with Baalis (40:14). They observe that the king’s daughters may be daughters of the royal house generally rather than of Zedekiah alone, and they hold such identifications loosely as the text allows.
